The '''Schulz–Zimm distribution''' is a special case of the [[gamma distribution]]. It is widely used to model the [[polydispersity]] of [[polymer]]s. In this context it has been introduced in 1939 by [[Günter Victor Schulz]]<ref>G V Schulz (1939), Z. Phys. Chem. 43B, 25-46. - Eq (27a) with -ln(''a''), ''k''+1 in place of our ''x,k''.</ref> and in 1948 by [[Bruno H. Zimm]].<ref>B H Zimm (1948), J. Chem. Phys. 16, 1099. - Proposes a two-parameter variant of Eq (13) without derivation and without reference to Schulz or whomsoever. One of the two parameters can be eliminated by the requirement <n>=1.</ref>

This distribution has only a shape parameter ''k'', the scale being fixed at ''&theta;''=1/''k''. Accordingly, the probability density function is
<math display="block">f(x)=\frac{k^k x^{k - 1} e^{-kx}}{\Gamma(k)}, </math> where ''&Gamma;(x)'' is the [[Gamma function]].

When applied to polymers, the variable ''x'' is the relative mass or chain length <math>x=M/M_n</math>. Accordingly, the mass distribution <math>f(M)</math> is just a gamma distribution with scale parameter <math>\theta=M_n/k</math>. This explains why the Schulz–Zimm distribution is unheard of outside its conventional application domain.

The distribution has mean 1 and variance 1/''k''. The polymer dispersity is <math>\langle x^2\rangle / \langle x\rangle = 1+1/k</math>.

For large ''k'' the Schulz–Zimm distribution approaches a [[Gaussian distribution]]. In algorithms where one needs to draw samples <math>x\ge 0</math>, the Schulz–Zimm distribution is to be preferred over a Gaussian because the latter requires an arbitrary cut-off to prevent negative ''x''.
